transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, well, honestly I wasn't even planning on coming in, but the people at the regular clinic just kept getting on my case. They’ve been really on me about how little I’ve been eating lately. Which, I mean, I guess I don't eat a ton, but my schedule is just so crazy. Like, I work at the warehouse, packing and taping boxes all day, and I have to be there super early. So most days, I’m just grabbing a coffee before my shift starts, because who really has time or the stomach for breakfast at that hour? 

And then I’m on my feet all day, and right after work I have to rush over to my GED classes—I'm trying to finally finish that up, you know, so I can maybe get a better job eventually. So by the time I get out of there, maybe I’ll have a yogurt or just, like, a few bites of something small when I get home. It's just... I don't know, sitting down for an actual, real meal just feels like it throws off everything. It feels like it ruins my whole routine and everything I’m trying so hard to keep in line. If I stop and eat a big plate of food, it just messes up my whole momentum and how I feel in my body. So I just stick to what works for me, but the clinic made it sound like this huge issue, so... here I am.
Have you noticed any significant weight loss recently, or do you consider your weight to be lower than what’s healthy for you?

I mean... yeah, I guess the number on the scale has gone down. But I wouldn't call it, like, a bad thing? It’s just... well, for example, my work pants—the thick canvas ones I have to wear at the warehouse—they're definitely really loose on me now. I’ve had to start pulling my belt on the absolute tightest notch, which honestly is kind of annoying because when you're bending over and lifting and taping heavy boxes for eight hours, the extra fabric just bunches up around the waist and rubs against you. 

But anyway, yeah, people at work have been saying stuff, and the nurses at the clinic too, always telling me I look "too thin" or asking if I'm feeling okay. They just won't drop it. But the thing is, when I actually step on the scale in the morning—which I always do right before I head out the door, it's just a strict habit for me now—and I see that number go down... I don't know, it feels like I’m finally getting somewhere. Like I’m actually making progress on something, you know? Especially when my job is just so repetitive and I'm still just trying to get through these GED classes after all these years. Seeing that number drop gives me something to actually feel good about, like I'm in control. 

So when people tell me it's not healthy, or they try to pressure me into changing what I'm doing... I just don’t see why I should be pushed to put the weight back on. It makes zero sense to me. Why would I want to undo all that when I finally feel like I'm succeeding at something?
Do you ever feel afraid of gaining weight or becoming fat, even if others might tell you that you're already underweight?

I mean, yeah, I do. I really do. It’s... it's constantly on my mind, honestly. Like, even just the thought of gaining the weight back makes my stomach tie itself into knots. Because, you know, sometimes at work, somebody will bring in donuts or, like, fried chicken from the place down the street for a birthday or something, and they just leave it in the break room. And it smells so strong, and people are always like, "Oh, come on, just have a piece, you're working so hard." Or like on Sundays, when I go to church, they always have this huge potluck afterward. And the ladies there, they just pile your plate high with casserole and rolls and dessert, and they watch you to make sure you eat it. 

And if I actually give in and eat something like that—like, say I have a piece of that fried chicken or I eat a big plate of whatever they're serving at church—I just immediately panic. I get this horrible, overwhelming fear that it’s going to show on my body right away. Like, I’ll literally feel like my thighs are getting bigger or my stomach is poking out just from that one meal. And I can't stop thinking about it. It just replays in my head over and over, like, "Why did you eat that? You ruined everything." And the only thing that makes me feel even a little bit better is knowing I can check the scale. I’ll just be sitting there in GED class or back on the warehouse floor, and all I want to do is run home and step on the scale just to see how much damage I did. Because if I don't know the number, the fear just kind of eats me alive. So, yeah, even if people say I'm too thin, the idea of getting fat again... it terrifies me. It really does.

After eating something you feel is high in calories or more than you wanted, do you ever make yourself exercise a lot more, make yourself vomit, or do anything else to try to 'undo' the food or keep from gaining weight?

No, I don't really do anything like that. I mean, I know some people do those kinds of things, like making themselves sick or taking pills or whatever, but that's just... I couldn't do that. Honestly, the thought of throwing up just grosses me out so much, I can't even imagine making myself do it on purpose. And as for exercising, well, like I said, I'm on my feet all day at the warehouse. I'm constantly walking back and forth, lifting boxes, taping them up, moving pallets... it's exhausting work. By the time I get off my shift and then sit through my GED classes, my feet are just throbbing and my back aches. 

So the idea of going for a run or hitting a gym after all that? It's just not going to happen. I don't have the energy, and frankly, I don't have the time or the money for a gym membership anyway. I just try to stick to my routine, you know? Just... control what I put in my mouth in the first place, so I don't have to worry about trying to undo it later. Because if I just don't eat the bad things, then I don't have to panic about it. It's just easier to restrict it upfront than to try to fix it after the fact. So, yeah, no throwing up or crazy workouts or anything like that. Just... trying to be careful. Very, very careful.
